Edgar. The legitimate son of the Earl of Gloucester in Shakespeare's King Lear, whose inheritance and sanity are stolen by his illegitimate half-brother Edmund. Falsely accused of plotting against his father, Edgar flees and disguises himself as a madman, becoming the instrument of his father's punishment and, eventually, his salvation. His tragic arc from innocent heir to exile to redemption mirrors and complicates the play's central themes of family betrayal and the nature of legitimacy. Edgar is the rightful heir to Gloucester's estate until Edmund's ruthless schemes displace him and cunningly turn their father against him through calculated deception. Edmund forges a letter in Edgar's hand to convince Gloucester that Edgar is plotting regicide and patricide against his father, leading to Edgar's wrongful banishment and exile from home. Disguised as Poor Tom, a beggar driven mad by desperation and despair, Edgar becomes the instrument through which Gloucester's blindness—both literal and metaphorical moral blindness—is ultimately exposed. Gloucester's blinding at the hands of his political tormentors occurs after he belatedly discovers Edmund's terrible treachery, and it is Edgar, still disguised and unrecognized, who saves him from suicidal despair. The revelation of Edgar's innocence comes painfully late, after extensive suffering and psychological torment, aligning with the play's persistently bleak vision of justice, redemption, and familial trust. Edgar's survival and return to authority at the play's end suggests possible redemption and restoration, though the devastating cost of his suffering fundamentally undercuts any simple or optimistic reading of recovery. His disguise as Poor Tom allows him to experience society from the bottom, gaining both humility and moral wisdom that eventually qualify him to rule with justice and understanding. In the end, Edgar shares a father with Edmund through their mutual parentage, yet their characters could not be more different, defining the play's obsession with how legitimacy and illegitimacy shape the soul.
